stem: Which figure is used as the base when calculating inventory turnover in days?

options.content: Cost of sales
options.rationale: Correct: inventory is valued at cost.

options.content: Revenue
options.rationale: Revenue includes profit; inventory is held at cost.

options.content: Credit purchases
options.rationale: That is the base for payables days.

options.content: Gross profit
options.rationale: Gross profit is not the cost of the goods.

explanation: Inventory days = average (or closing) inventory ÷ cost of sales × 365.

stem: Trade receivables days are calculated by dividing trade receivables by:

options.content: credit sales, then multiplying by 365
options.rationale: Correct: only credit sales create trade receivables.

options.content: cost of sales, then multiplying by 365
options.rationale: Cost of sales is the base for inventory days.

options.content: credit purchases, then multiplying by 365
options.rationale: That is the base for payables days.

options.content: total assets, then multiplying by 365
options.rationale: Total assets are not related to credit customers.

explanation: Trade receivables days = trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365.

stem: Trade payables days measure the average time taken to:

options.content: collect cash from customers who bought on credit
options.rationale: That is trade receivables days.

options.content: sell the inventory held at the year end
options.rationale: That is inventory days.

options.content: repay the loan notes that are due in five years
options.rationale: Loan notes are not trade payables.

options.content: pay suppliers for goods bought on credit
options.rationale: Correct: calculated from trade payables and credit purchases.

explanation: Trade payables days = trade payables ÷ credit purchases × 365.

stem: A company's trade receivables days rose from 35 to 58 although its credit terms are 30 days. What is the most likely cause?

options.content: Better credit control, with customers paying early
options.rationale: Early payment would reduce the days.

options.content: A fall in the volume of credit purchases
options.rationale: Purchases do not affect receivables days.

options.content: Weak credit control, with customers paying late
options.rationale: Correct: collection is far slower than the terms allow.

options.content: A fall in the cost of sales
options.rationale: Cost of sales is not used in this ratio.

explanation: Receivables days well above the credit period suggest customers are not paying on time, so credit control is weak.
hints: Compare the figure with the credit period given.

stem: A shop's inventory turnover rose from 6 times to 8 times a year. Which statement is most likely to be true?

options.content: Inventory is being sold more slowly, so inventory days have risen
options.rationale: That would reduce the number of times.

options.content: Inventory is being sold more quickly, so inventory days have fallen
options.rationale: Correct: higher turnover means fewer days to sell.

options.content: The shop is holding more inventory to support the same level of sales
options.rationale: More inventory for the same cost of sales lowers the turnover.

options.content: Credit customers are paying more slowly than in the earlier year
options.rationale: Receivables do not affect inventory turnover.

explanation: Inventory turnover in times and in days are two views of the same speed: more times a year means fewer days.
hints: Times and days move in opposite directions.

stem: Which action is most likely to reduce a company's trade receivables days?

options.content: Extending the credit period given to customers from 30 to 60 days
options.rationale: That would increase the days.

options.content: Offering a discount to customers who pay within 10 days
options.rationale: Correct: it encourages earlier payment, at a cost.

options.content: Paying suppliers earlier in the month than before
options.rationale: That affects payables days, not receivables.

options.content: Buying more inventory from suppliers on credit terms
options.rationale: That affects inventory and payables.

explanation: A cash discount gives customers a reason to pay early; it shortens receivables days but costs the discount.
hints: Which action gets customers to pay sooner?

stem: Revenue rose by 5% but non-current asset turnover fell, because a new factory was completed late in the year. What is the best explanation?

options.content: Revenue fell relative to the cost of sales in the same year
options.rationale: The ratio uses revenue and non-current assets only.

options.content: Depreciation was not charged on the new factory in the year
options.rationale: That would raise the carrying amount, but it is not the stated cause.

options.content: The company collected its trade receivables more quickly
options.rationale: Receivables are current assets and are not in this ratio.

options.content: The carrying amount of non-current assets rose faster than revenue
options.rationale: Correct: the new factory raised the denominator before it produced sales.

explanation: A new asset adds to non-current assets at once, while its revenue builds up only gradually, so the turnover falls at first.
hints: Which part of the fraction increased most?

stem: A longer time to sell inventory always means higher profit because prices can be raised.
explanation: False. A longer holding period ties up cash and risks damage or obsolescence; it does not raise profit.

stem: A rise in trade payables days improves a business's cash position in the short term.
explanation: True. Paying suppliers later keeps cash in the business, although suppliers may withdraw credit or discounts.

stem: Match each ratio to its formula.
explanation: Each ratio compares a balance with the flow that creates it: cost of sales for inventory, credit sales for receivables, credit purchases for payables.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Rate of inventory turnover is cost of sales divided by {{blank:a}} inventory. A longer period of {{blank:b}} days means customers are paying more slowly.

explanation: The Cambridge appendix divides cost of sales by average inventory; slower collection shows as higher receivables days.

stem: By what number are inventory, receivables and payables ratios multiplied to give a figure in days?
explanation: The balance is divided by the annual flow and multiplied by 365 days.

stem: A company's cost of sales for the year was US\$311,000 and its revenue was US\$428,000. Closing inventory was US\$47,300. Using the closing inventory, calculate inventory turnover in days to the nearest whole day.
explanation: 47,300 ÷ 311,000 × 365 = 56 days. Using revenue as the base would give 40 days.
workedSolution: 1. 47,300 ÷ 311,000 × 365 = 56 days. Using revenue as the base would give 40 days.

stem: A company had revenue of US\$470,000, of which US\$352,000 was on credit. Trade receivables at the year end were US\$63,400. Calculate trade receivables days to the nearest whole day.
explanation: 63,400 ÷ 352,000 × 365 = 66 days. Using total revenue would give 49 days and understate the delay.
workedSolution: 1. 63,400 ÷ 352,000 × 365 = 66 days. Using total revenue would give 49 days and understate the delay.
hints: Use credit sales, not total revenue.

stem: Inventory was US\$38,600 at 1 January and US\$45,400 at 31 December. Cost of sales for the year was US\$301,140. Calculate the rate of inventory turnover in times, using average inventory, to one decimal place.
explanation: Average inventory = (38,600 + 45,400) ÷ 2 = 42,000. Turnover = 301,140 ÷ 42,000 = 7.2 times. Using the closing figure alone gives 6.6 times.
workedSolution: 1. Average inventory = (38,600 + 45,400) ÷ 2 = 42,000. Turnover = 301,140 ÷ 42,000 = 7.2 times. Using the closing figure alone gives 6.6 times.

stem: ZIMSEC style. Total assets turnover = revenue ÷ total assets. A company's revenue was US\$560,800 and its total assets were US\$412,000, of which current assets were US\$138,000. Calculate total assets turnover in times to two decimal places.
explanation: 560,800 ÷ 412,000 = 1.36 times. Dividing by current assets would give current assets turnover, 4.06 times.
workedSolution: 1. 560,800 ÷ 412,000 = 1.36 times. Dividing by current assets would give current assets turnover, 4.06 times.
hints: Use total assets, not current assets.

stem: Explain why a business may want its trade payables days to be longer than its trade receivables days.

points.description: It receives cash from customers before it has to pay its suppliers
Suppliers then finance part of the working capital, so less bank finance is needed

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: If customers pay before the suppliers are paid, the supplier credit finances the business, and the business needs less cash or overdraft to run.

explanation: One mark for the timing and one for the effect on finance.

stem: A company's inventory days fell from 62 to 40. Give two possible benefits and one possible danger.

points.description: Benefit 1: less cash is tied up in inventory
Benefit 2: lower storage costs and less risk of damage or obsolescence
Danger: running out of items, losing sales and customers
A judgement that the improvement is worthwhile only if sales are not lost

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Faster stock turnover frees cash and cuts storage costs and the risk of obsolete items. The danger is stock-outs that lose sales, so it is good only if customers can still buy what they want.

explanation: Two marks for benefits, one for the danger and one for the judgement.
hints: Think of both cash and customers.

stem: A company reduced its trade payables days from 48 to 31 in a year when its receivables days rose from 40 to 55. Explain the effect on the company and suggest one action.

points.description: Customers take longer to pay while suppliers are paid sooner
Cash is absorbed twice: less supplier finance and more cash tied up in receivables
The company may need an overdraft, which has a finance cost
Suppliers may now be demanding earlier payment, or the company is taking early-payment discounts
Action: stricter credit control or a discount for early payment; or negotiate longer supplier terms

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The company is paid more slowly and pays more quickly, so cash is squeezed from both sides and it may have to borrow. It should improve credit control or offer an early-payment discount, or ask suppliers for longer terms.

explanation: One mark each for the two movements, the effect on cash and finance, a possible cause and an action.
hints: Consider the cash effect of each change.

points.description: Payables days fell from 51 to 36: suppliers now finance less of the business
Receivables days rose from 49 to 55: customers pay more slowly
